title: Guests at midnight
hookLine: three men in student dress refuse Jarasandha's welcome; why a host's welcome is sacred in Hindu life
carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is god

lines: THE KING STANDS TO GREET THEM.
cards: Three men walk into the capital of Magadha dressed as snatakas, young brahmanas who've just finished their studies. They wear garlands and sandal paste.
They don't come in by the main gate, a strange way for students to arrive anywhere. And they walk straight into the king's presence. Jarasandha stands to receive them as honored guests.
He has no idea that Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna are standing in his hall.

teach.b: Jarasandha does everything a good host should: water, honors, a seat. They won't take it.
Krishna says his two companions are keeping a vow of silence until midnight. So the king leaves, comes back at midnight, and asks what he's been holding. Snatakas don't wear garlands like this.
Your arms are marked like the arms of men who draw bows. You came in by a wrong way, and you refused my worship. Who are you?
Krishna answers carefully. A snataka enters a friend's house by its gate, and an enemy's by another way. And we don't accept worship from an enemy.
Then he names the wrong: you've captured kings to offer them up.
We've come to free them. And he tells the king exactly who they are. Why refuse the welcome?
Because in Hindu life a host's welcome is close to holy.

The Taittiriya Upanishad puts it in a line still taught to children across India: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be God to you. Water, a seat, food: that's how you'd receive a god, and it's how you receive a guest.
Many readers say taking that honor binds a guest to his host, so Krishna won't accept it from a man he's come to fight. He'd rather look strange than be false. Jarasandha answers just as plainly.
I took those kings in war, and I won't let them go out of fear. Fight me, one of you, or two, or all three.
He looks them over, and chooses Bhima.

how: A Hindu host traditionally offers a guest water, a seat and food, and the Taittiriya Upanishad's 'atithi devo bhava', let the guest be God to you, is still taught across India. A snataka is a student who has finished Vedic study and taken the bath that ends it.

o: a vow of silence kept until the stroke of midnight
the ritual bath that ends a student's Vedic study
the royal rite whose road runs through Jarasandha's hall

games.q: the midnight meeting — tap the pairs.
p: let the guest be God to you

s: the three refused Jarasandha's offered worship
Krishna says they won't accept worship from an enemy.
refusing the welcome was just rudeness
a host's welcome is close to holy; Krishna wouldn't take it from a man he'd come to fight.
Krishna kept their identity secret to the end
once asked, he named all three and said why they'd come.

games.q: you're Krishna. Jarasandha offers water, honors and a seat. you've come to fight him. what do you do?
o: refuse, since a host's welcome is sacred.
games.why: he refuses: a snataka takes no worship from a foe. where the guest is God, you don't take a welcome you mean to break.

practice: Hindu homes greet a guest with water first. Before you sit, set out a glass of water as if someone you love were about to walk in.

Then close your eyes and picture the next people who'll come through your door, the easy one and the difficult one, and see yourself greeting each as if God had come. If you pray, ask for a welcome that's honest.
If you don't, just ask yourself what an honest welcome would look like.

wordCard.voice: The Rajasuya. Today its road runs through Jarasandha's hall at midnight, where three guests refuse his welcome and tell him why they've come.

orig.note: Sanskrit snātaka: a student who has completed study and taken the bath that ends it; the dress Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna wear.

carryVoice: Your line: atithi devo bhava, the guest is God. Krishna wouldn't take a welcome he meant to break. That's day seven hundred fifty-four.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Jarasandha-vadha Parva (the journey to Girivraja in snataka dress; the vow of silence until midnight; Krishna's answer; Jarasandha chooses Bhima)
